questions.question: What happens when connector tasks arrive faster than the framework can execute them?
questions.answer: I would locate the real admission point and explain whether excess work is queued, rejected, delayed or bounded by the caller. ExecutorService alone does not define a safe overload policy. A finite queue protects memory but forces an explicit rejection or backpressure decision; an unbounded queue can turn overload into growing latency and resource exhaustion. I need [[HARSH TO FILL: actual executor queue, rejection behavior and upstream response]]. I would then describe how the token-bucket limiter and Resilience4j policies interact with this admission decision, if they do in the implementation. I would not assume a limiter controls concurrency or that a circuit breaker controls request rate. The correct policy depends on job durability and caller expectations.

followups.q: Does a token bucket cap concurrent work?
followups.a: Not inherently; it limits starts over time, while concurrency needs a separate bound.

followups.q: What if rejected work must not be lost?
followups.a: Persist or return it through a durable retry contract rather than silently dropping it.

questions.trap: Treating rate limiting, thread-pool capacity and circuit breaking as interchangeable controls.
questions.notes: Concurrency status stays SHAKY pending a coherent personal mechanism.

questions.question: Which Resilience4j policies did your project use, and how did you avoid harmful retry amplification?
questions.answer: The project description names Resilience4j but not which modules or configuration were implemented. I would identify the actual policy around one dependency, its purpose, its thresholds and the failure categories it sees. If retries exist, I would state attempt limits, delay behavior, deadline budget and idempotency requirements, then explain whether a circuit breaker observes each attempt or the final operation. I need [[HARSH TO FILL: actual policy, configuration and test evidence]]. Policies can amplify load when each layer retries independently, so I would trace the full call stack and calculate the total attempt bound only from real settings. If the feature is merely planned, I would say that instead of claiming it shipped.

followups.q: Should every transient exception be retried?
followups.a: No. Consider operation safety, remaining deadline, provider guidance and total attempt budget.

followups.q: How do you validate breaker transitions?
followups.a: Use focused tests with controlled outcomes and verify the actual configured state behavior.

questions.trap: Name-dropping Resilience4j without identifying the configured policies or their failure semantics.
questions.notes: No Resilience4j module or numeric setting inferred.

questions.question: Explain the token-bucket rate limiter in your framework, including its state and burst behavior.
questions.answer: The resume names token-bucket rate limiting, so I would explain the actual bucket's capacity, refill rule, request cost and decision when insufficient tokens exist. A token bucket permits bounded bursts while controlling average admission over time; it does not by itself cap simultaneous in-flight operations. I need [[HARSH TO FILL: implementation location, state model, refill clock and rejection or wait behavior]]. If multiple application instances share a limit, I would state whether state is local or coordinated and what consistency trade-off follows. I would cover clock behavior and tests around refill boundaries. No rate, capacity or measured result is supplied, so I must not invent numeric settings or claim a specific distributed algorithm.

followups.q: What does bucket capacity control?
followups.a: The maximum stored tokens and therefore the permitted burst, based on its configured semantics.

followups.q: Can a local bucket enforce one global limit?
followups.a: Not across independent instances without coordination; each local bucket maintains separate state.

questions.trap: Inventing bucket parameters or describing rate limit as a concurrency limit.
questions.notes: Mechanism detail is requested but not present in supplied facts.

questions.question: How does the Redis token cache behave on a miss, expiry, concurrent refresh or Redis outage?
questions.answer: The project description says it uses a Redis token cache but supplies no key design or fallback policy. I would explain the real cache key scope, token expiry margin, refresh ownership and whether concurrent misses are coalesced. Then I would distinguish a cache miss from a Redis outage and state whether the system can obtain a token safely without Redis. I need [[HARSH TO FILL: key dimensions, TTL rule, refresh lock or coordination and outage behavior]]. Tokens are sensitive, so I would cover access controls, transport and logging without exposing values. Tests should exercise expiry and simultaneous refresh. I would avoid claiming cache invalidation, global coordination or availability guarantees that the project has not actually implemented.

followups.q: Should a token TTL exceed its real expiry?
followups.a: No. The cache should not serve a token beyond its validity; any safety margin must match actual policy.

followups.q: Does Redis availability equal identity-provider availability?
followups.a: No. They are separate dependencies with distinct failure and recovery behavior.

questions.trap: Assuming Redis cache behavior or fallback semantics not stated in the project facts.
questions.notes: Cache mechanism remains placeholder-led.

questions.question: How does one connector's slow or failing dependency affect other connector work in the framework?
questions.answer: I would trace whether connectors share an executor, connection pool, rate limit or downstream client, since any shared bounded resource can create cross-provider interference. Isolation might use per-provider bulkheads, separate budgets or fair admission, but those are design options rather than supplied implementation facts. I need [[HARSH TO FILL: shared resources, actual isolation policy and a failure test]]. I would identify the useful failure signal and the trade-off: more isolation can improve containment while increasing resource reservation and operational complexity. A test should make one fake provider slow and verify the expected behavior of unrelated work. I would not claim the framework isolates failures just because each provider has a separate Strategy implementation.

followups.q: Does a separate strategy imply separate execution capacity?
followups.a: No. Implementations can still share the same executor or downstream resources.

followups.q: What is the cost of per-provider pools?
followups.a: More reserved capacity and configuration, plus potential underutilization.

questions.trap: Confusing code modularity with runtime fault isolation.
questions.notes: No isolation mechanism or pool topology is assumed.

questions.question: How did you validate the Pluggable Connector Framework end to end, and what evidence would make you change its design?
questions.answer: I would demonstrate one representative connector path from selection through execution, result handling and a failure case, then show the tests that protect each boundary. The project description names patterns, asynchronous execution, resilience, rate limiting and Redis caching, but gives no benchmark or deployment result. I need [[HARSH TO FILL: runnable scenario, test coverage, observed limitation and any measurement]]. I would explain what evidence might change the design, such as contention, unsafe retry behavior or a provider-specific capability that does not fit the contract. If it is a personal project, I would state its scope and avoid representing it as production client infrastructure. I would separate implemented behavior from future work throughout the answer.

followups.q: What is the strongest current evidence?
followups.a: Name a reproducible test or measurement actually available: [[HARSH TO FILL: evidence]].

followups.q: What would you avoid claiming?
followups.a: Production scale, reliability or adoption without real deployment evidence.

questions.trap: Presenting a list of technologies as proof of a tested or production-ready framework.
questions.notes: Completes project defense without asserting deployment or scale.

questions.question: What are the disadvantages of your project's architecture?
questions.answer: The interviewer wants honest engineering judgement, structured as trade-off, impact and what you would change, followed by what you actually improved. For my project the real answer is [[HARSH TO FILL: the actual weaknesses of the architecture I work on and the measured result of any fix]]. Typical weakness patterns, to use only if true for my system, are synchronous chains between services that cause cascading latency, with non-critical steps better moved to events; two services sharing a database, which couples their deployments; missing timeouts or circuit breakers so one slow dependency exhausts a connection pool; retries without idempotency creating duplicates; and missing tracing, which makes debugging slow. Close with the improvement and its measurable outcome.

followups.q: How do you keep the answer from sounding like a complaint?
followups.a: Name the trade-off, quantify its impact and finish with what you changed and the result.

followups.q: Which weaknesses should you avoid claiming?
followups.a: Any you did not actually see or fix; invented examples fall apart under follow-up questions.

questions.trap: Inventing generic weaknesses that are not true of your system.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 7.19 (Accolite). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S19-002, JH-S20-042.
